Claim and who made it: Ambjent Malta told the Times of Malta (1 Oct 2026) that because the concrete in the tree planters is temporary, it will not damage the tree.
Counter-evidence or context: Ambjent itself says prolonged cover would be a concern. No duration for 'temporary' is given; soil removal and root exposure are not addressed; no tree-specific evidence published.
Test it against: Soil-sealing and construction-damage literature; guidance on exposed roots.
Why it is low-hanging: Done: Claim Check 001 report and flyer.
Caveats: Draft pending right of reply. Verdict is plausible-but-unproven: no study found on short-term concrete contact with roots; Ambjent's own reasoning is consistent with the literature.
Notes: Report v1.1; verdict Not substantiated (moderate); right of reply to send (draft; not for circulation before the deadline).

Claim and who made it: ERA (11 Aug 2026): 54 protected trees will be removed, with 10 new indigenous trees planted for each (540). Of 678 trees and shrubs to be removed, 92% are classified as non-protected; 348 more are to be transplanted.
Counter-evidence or context: The published figures describe proposed interventions and planting conditions, not completed work or measured ecological replacement. Studies show that transplant outcomes vary with species, source, site suitability and aftercare; tree counts alone do not establish survival, habitat recovery or equivalent ecological function.
Test it against: Recalculate ERA's count and ratio; distinguish the removal, transplantation and pruning categories; compare species-level local ecological evidence with plant-translocation and mature-tree studies; identify what monitoring would demonstrate survival and recovery. Do not assess the permit's legal merits.
Why it is low-hanging: ERA's direct statement gives verifiable counts; the ecological outcome needs independent, species-specific follow-up data.
Caveats: This check assesses the scientific meaning of the reported tree counts and proposed mitigation only. It does not assess permit validity or any tribunal proceedings. The tree works and planting had not been independently verified as completed at the 3 October 2026 cut-off. ERA and secondary reporting differ by one oleander in the breakdown of the 624 non-protected specimens (467 versus 468); the permit annex should be checked before treating that species count as settled. No right of reply needed (verdict Largely supported; a reply is sought only for Not substantiated, Misleading or Contradicted).
Notes: Report v1.0; verdict Largely supported (moderate); no right of reply needed.

Claim and who made it: Climate Action Authority (13 Nov 2025): emissions per capita have fallen 44% since 2005, well above the EU average of 34%, showing Malta is reducing emissions at household level and across the economy.
Counter-evidence or context: The same Commission report shows effort-sharing emissions 41% above 2005 in 2024 and projects +42% (existing measures) or +30% (planned measures) by 2030 against a -19% target: the largest gap in the EU in percentage points. Malta was over its yearly ESR limit by 22, 25 and 30 points in 2022-2024 (+43/+42/+41% vs +21/+16/+11%); the 2021 surplus carried forward brings the cumulative balance to 0.0 Mt in 2024, -2.1 Mt projected for 2030 before flexibilities. Total emissions fell 27% (EU 33%); population grew 41%, explaining about half the per-person fall. Among the EU-27 (2005-2024) Malta ranks 3rd on the per-person cut (-48.5%) but 20th on the total cut (-27.4%). Transport +49%, F-gases about six-fold. In the authority's favour: effort-sharing emissions per person are flat (2.50 t in 2005, 2.52 t in 2024; proxy: total minus power generation), and no compliance shortfall has arisen before the first check in 2027.
Test it against: Eurostat env_air_gge and nama_10_pe (Malta, EU-27 aggregate and all 27 Member States); Commission CAPR 2025 SWD Tables 25 and 26; Eurostat nrg_ind_ren.
Why it is low-hanging: Done: Claim Check 003 report and flyer.
Body / actor: Climate Action Authority; Ministry for the Environment
Caveats: Draft pending right of reply (Climate Action Authority; Environment Ministry). Misleading must not be published before the reply deadline passes. Figures accurate; verdict rests on omission of the 2030 projection from the report the authority cites.
Notes: Report v1.2; verdict Misleading (high); right of reply to send (draft; not for circulation before the deadline).

Claim and who made it: Ministry for the Environment (19 Jan 2026): Malta continues to make strong progress in waste management; mixed waste down over 30% to 95.5 million kg; about 412 million kg diverted from landfill over five years; the Long-Term Waste Management Plan is working.
Counter-evidence or context: Municipal recycling rate 16.7% in 2024 (EU 48.1%; 2025 target 55%), second-lowest of the 20 states with 2024 data; 79% of treated municipal waste landfilled. The Commission's 2023 early-warning report lists Malta among 10 states at risk of missing both 2025 targets and 13 far from the 2035 landfill target; its 2025 review says Malta missed the 2020 target by a large margin and is on course to miss 2025. Malta notified a postponement in December 2023 and renounced it in November 2024. Treated biowaste is used for landscaping and landfill remediation and reported as landfilled. The 412 million kg cannot be reconciled with Eurostat (271 kt recycled or recovered, 2020-24); the 141 million kg baseline has no year. In fairness, the rate rose 7.6 points 2019-2024 (4th-largest rise of 20 EU states) and packaging recycling rose from 30.8% to 43.4% in 2023. (ERA's 68% figure is explicitly for construction waste and is not part of this claim.)
Test it against: Eurostat cei_wm011 (Malta and all EU-27), env_wasmun, cei_wm020; NSO releases; Directive (EU) 2018/851 Art 11a; Commission COM(2023) 304, SWD(2023) 195 and SWD(2025) 318.
Why it is low-hanging: Done: Claim Check 004 report and flyer (v1.1).
Body / actor: Ministry for the Environment, Energy and Public Cleanliness (Minister Dalli); WasteServ
Caveats: Draft pending right of reply (Environment Ministry; WasteServ). The ministry may hold operational data that explain the 412 figure; 2025 statistics not yet published. The link between the deposit refund scheme and the 2023 packaging jump is our inference; the scheme's 78% collected and 74% recycled (2023) are reported by the Commission from ERA and were not recomputed.
Notes: Report v1.1; verdict Not substantiated (high); right of reply to send (draft; not for circulation before the deadline).

Claim and who made it: Malta also shows excellent records under the Bathing Water Directive: 92% of Maltese bathing waters are of excellent quality.
Counter-evidence or context: The EEA series shows a decline: 86 of 87 sites were excellent in 2016–2018 (98.9%), then 85, 84, 84, 82, 80, 80 and 77 (88.5%) in 2025, the lowest of the eleven seasons since 2015. Malta's lead over the EU-27 coastal average (88.3% in 2025) fell from about 11 percentage points in 2016 to 0.2. Ten of the 87 sites account for every rating below excellent; in 2025 St George's Bay B03 (St Julian's) and Xlendi D06 and D07 fell from excellent to good. Balluta Bay's two sites (B08, B09) were rated only sufficient in every season 2022–2025, with a sewage-related warning from late May to 12 August 2024 inside that run. The CJEU found failures to comply with urban wastewater treatment obligations in named agglomerations. None of this refutes the Commission's figure, which was correct for 2023 and again for 2024, but the summary sentence gives no year.
Test it against: Confirm the Commission's exact wording and reference year; reproduce the count from the EEA's per-site classifications for every season 2015–2025 (map service, checked site by site against the WISE dataset) and compare with the EU-27 coastal share; identify the sites behind each change; establish what the Bathing Water Directive classification measures; distinguish multi-season classification from short-term warnings and from urban wastewater treatment compliance.
Why it is low-hanging: The Commission’s precise 2023 indicator is verifiable, while the omission of its reference year and the newer 2025 result can make it sound current.
Caveats: Supported applies to the quoted statistic, which was the 2023 result (80/87) and was repeated in 2024. The 2025 classification is 88.5%, the lowest since 2015. This indicator uses E. coli and intestinal enterococci over four seasons of samples and is not a general assessment of marine ecological or chemical status. No right of reply needed (verdict Supported; a reply is sought only for Not substantiated, Misleading or Contradicted).
Notes: Report v1.2; verdict Supported (high); no right of reply needed.

Claim and who made it: Malta’s 2026 spring-hunting derogation met the Birds Directive’s “small numbers” and strict-supervision conditions, with quotas of 2,400 Quail and 1,500 Turtle-doves.
Counter-evidence or context: The 2025 WBRU outcome report documents enforcement activity and offences, but it cannot establish how the 2026 season was supervised. The 2026 season outcome report was not available at review.
Test it against: Compare each 2026 quota with the mortality benchmark calculated in the legal notices; assess what the rules and available enforcement evidence show about supervision; keep legal benchmark compliance separate from ecological sustainability.
Why it is low-hanging: Drafted: statutory benchmarks recomputed and report/flyer produced. Right of reply remains for the maintainer.
Caveats: The statutory “small numbers” estimate is a modelled benchmark, not an independent estimate of the number of birds migrating through Malta or the effect of the hunt. Right of reply remains for the maintainer.
Notes: Report v1.1; verdict Not substantiated (moderate); right of reply to send (draft; not for circulation before the deadline).

Short title: Within EU limits vs WHO guideline
Claim and who made it: Newsbook (18 Jul 2025), reporting Parliamentary Question 29696: measurements taken between 2020 and 2024 at ERA's five PM2.5 monitoring stations are well above the WHO guideline but well within the less stringent EU annual limits.
Counter-evidence or context: All 23 reported station-year values exceed the WHO annual PM2.5 guideline of 5 µg/m³ and are below the EU annual limit of 25 µg/m³ applicable in 2020-2024. The annex marks St Paul's Bay as n/a for 2020 and 2021. Fourteen of 23 values exceed the EU limit of 10 µg/m³ due by 2030; this future standard does not establish past non-compliance. EEA validated daily data independently cross-check 11 station-years; ten match the annex to 0.1 µg/m³. Attard 2024 differs (12.122 µg/m³ from the EEA valid-day mean versus 11.9 in the annex), though both remain below 25 µg/m³.
Test it against: Parliamentary station means against the WHO 2021 annual guideline, the EU annual limit applicable in each data year, and the separate EU 2030 standard. Missing values and the Minister's exact answer are checked explicitly. Cross-check valid EEA daily aggregates against the rounded annex values and report completeness for available station-years.
Why it is low-hanging: 'Within EU limits' is a legal comparison, not a general health assessment; the official table is directly testable.
Caveats: The PQ answer only says the table is being laid before Parliament; it does not claim the table demonstrates compliance. Newsbook's report was read in full from its Wayback snapshot (4 Oct 2026). St Paul's Bay has no reported value for 2020 or 2021. The EEA validated data cross-check reproduces 10 of 11 available values to one decimal; Attard 2024 is 12.122 µg/m³ in the retrieved daily series versus 11.9 in the annex. Both remain below the applicable EU limit. The result does not show the air is healthy, infer individual health effects, or treat the 2030 EU standard as a limit for prior years.
Notes: Report v1.2; verdict Largely supported (high); no right of reply needed.

Claim and who made it: Infrastructure Malta says the Msida Creek flyover will reduce delays, emissions and noise, and that the Marsa Junction Project has reduced travel time and air pollution.
Counter-evidence or context: The Msida Creek flyover opened to traffic on 18 December 2025, and the wider project remains under construction until 2027. At the only public air monitor near it (EEA sampling point MT00011, about 410 m away), mean NO2 for January–September 2026 was 25.2 µg/m³, against 22.0 in 2025 and 19.2 in 2024 (2026 data not yet validated); urban background stations rose about 4% and St Paul's Bay fell 6%, so the expected improvement has not appeared in the measured data. The Marsa release does not link the surveys behind its percentage claims, and no EEA-reported air monitor has operated within 1.4 km of the Marsa junction since Kordin (Paola) closed at the end of 2016. No project-level before-and-after series was found for traffic or noise at either site.
Test it against: Separate forecasts from measured outcomes for Msida and Marsa; inspect the planning baseline and public monitoring record; compare hourly EEA NO2 at the Msida monitor with background and traffic stations for January–September 2024, 2025 and 2026 (before and after the flyover opened); locate the monitoring points from ERA's station metadata; assess what induced-demand research can and cannot infer for these individual junctions.
Why it is low-hanging: Official wording and project dates are available; outcome data need to be requested or located.
Caveats: The 79% travel-time and emissions reductions are Infrastructure Malta’s reported figures; their underlying survey design, time windows, calculation methods and raw results were not located. The Msida NO2 comparison rests on one monitor about 410 m from the flyover, a sampling point that replaced the old one (about 300 m west) in January 2024, unvalidated 2026 data, and no adjustment for weather or traffic; works continue until 2027, so it does not show that the flyover raised pollution. No post-project noise dataset was found for either site. The induced-demand literature cited is from US urban road networks and is not a direct estimate for Malta. Right of reply not sought, at the maintainer’s direction.
Notes: Report v1.2; verdict Not substantiated (moderate); right of reply to send (draft; not for circulation before the deadline).

Claim and who made it: WSC reported that reverse osmosis supplied 70.7% of its potable-water production in 2025, while groundwater production fell to 11.5 million m³, its lowest annual total in a decade. In August 2026, WSC issued a tender for a new 30,000 m³/day reverse-osmosis plant at Għar Lapsi.
Counter-evidence or context: The latest published River Basin Management Plan classifies both Malta and Gozo Mean Sea Level aquifer systems in poor quantitative status and 14 groundwater bodies in poor chemical status. Malta's reporting of the same cycle to the EEA lists four bodies in poor quantitative status (adding Pwales Coastal and Marfa Coastal) and all 15 in poor chemical status. The plan reports nitrate above the 50 mg/L standard in 12 of 15 bodies, with three named exceptions; not every body fails for nitrate. WSC's potable-production figures cover its supply system, not national abstraction. Eurostat estimates national fresh groundwater abstraction at 38.46 million m³ in 2024 (57% agriculture, up 3.1 million m³ on 2023), so WSC's 2025 cut of 1.55 million m³ is about 4% of it; a published water balance (Sapiano 2020) puts available groundwater at about 37 million m³ a year. Tracer ages of 15-40 years (Malta) and up to 60 or more (Gozo) mean water-quality recovery would take years to decades to show (Stuart et al. 2010).
Test it against: Recalculate RO shares and groundwater-production changes from WSC annual-report data; compare the WSC series with national abstraction and recharge (Eurostat env_wat_abs, env_wat_res) and with the regulator's separate groundwater-body quantity and chemistry assessments; read the peer-reviewed literature on Malta's aquifers; distinguish a tendered plant from commissioned capacity and measured aquifer recovery.
Why it is low-hanging: A rising desalinated-water share can reduce WSC's groundwater production, but it is not by itself proof that groundwater bodies have returned to good quantitative or chemical status.
Caveats: No right of reply needed (verdict Largely supported; a reply is sought only for Not substantiated, Misleading or Contradicted). WSC's 2025 annual report states that groundwater extraction fell 11.4% from 2024, while the annual-report chart values transcribed for 2024 and 2025 imply an 11.9% decline; the discrepancy is retained. WSC production is not a complete national groundwater- abstraction series; national abstraction and recharge are Eurostat estimates, and 2025 national figures are not yet published. The 3rd RBMP assessment period is older than the 2025 production figures, and a tender does not establish future operation or aquifer recovery. The plan's groundwater-body counts as recorded (Malta and Gozo Mean Sea Level poor quantitatively; 14 poor chemically) differ from Malta's 3rd-cycle EU reporting (4 and 15); the plan could not be re-opened to reconcile them, so the report shows both. "Lowest in a decade" is WSC's statement; the repo series covers 2022–2025 only. Stuart et al. (2010) was read as the authors' accepted manuscript; Mangion and Sapiano (2008) could not be read and is not used.
Notes: Report v1.2; verdict Largely supported (moderate); no right of reply needed.

Claim and who made it: Project Green reported more than 8,000 trees and more than 25,000 shrubs planted by government entities in 2024. Pledge 305 of the 2022 Labour manifesto commits to 100,000 trees being planted over the next five years; a February 2026 parliamentary answer reports around 60,000 trees and over 100,000 shrubs planted through the end of 2025.
Counter-evidence or context: Counts confirmed; the 100,000 trees were not reached by the end of 2025 (about 60,000), and no later count was found before the legislature ended on 30 May 2026. Maintainer decision (5 Oct 2026): delivery of 100,000 trees within the pledge period is rated separately as Not substantiated (sub-claim D); the overall verdict, on the reported counts, is unchanged. The reported 2024 and cumulative counts are planting inputs, not survival or canopy outcomes. The 2026 parliamentary answer says about 60,000 trees were planted by the end of 2025, below the 100,000 target at that date, when about 75% of the five-year window (from the 26 March 2022 election) had elapsed; Labour's 2026 manifesto gives a lower count of more than 57,000 trees for 2022-2025. The legislature ended with the snap general election of 30 May 2026; no count after 2025 was found (Project Green news to 5 Oct 2026, web searches). Tree and shrub totals are separate; vouchers are not trees planted.
Test it against: Check the exact pledge and its timeframe against official planting counts; separate trees from shrubs, trees planted from vouchers or supplied stock, and planted counts from survival, maintenance, removals and canopy change.
Why it is low-hanging: The headline totals are easy to check, but they do not show how many trees survived, where they were planted, or whether tree cover increased.
Body / actor: Project Green; Partit Laburista; Minister for the Environment
Caveats: The February 2026 answer gives a collective rounded total through end-2025 without project-level methods or a surviving-tree count. The legislature for which the pledge was made ended with the snap general election of 30 May 2026; no cumulative count after end-2025 was located (searched again 5 Oct 2026 for v1.2; parlament.mt returns 403 to scripts). The 2024 Project Green release and parliamentary answer report separate tree and shrub totals; do not combine them or treat them as canopy measures. Vouchers issued under the separate 2026 private-land scheme (23,000 trees by 13 May 2026) are not trees planted. Without a final count, the end-2025 figure does not prove a final shortfall either. Right of reply not sought, at the maintainer’s direction.
Notes: Report v1.2; verdict Largely supported (moderate); pledge Off track; right of reply to send (draft; not for circulation before the deadline).

Short title: Ten minutes' walk to green space
Claim and who made it: Labour manifesto 2026, priority 19: every person no more than ten minutes' walk from an open or green space. (Until v1.1 this check also covered the PN's net-zero Gozo pledge, now CC-107.)
Counter-evidence or context: Election held 30 May 2026; Labour won, so the pledge is now a government commitment. The manifesto defines neither "open or green space" nor a baseline or year. Our open-data analysis: 99.7-99.9% of residents already live within ten minutes of some green or open space, so read broadly the pledge is almost met; but only 55-68% live within a ten-minute walk of a public park of at least 0.5 ha (about 240,000 people outside), and 24% within 300 m of one (WHO Europe indicator).
Test it against: WorldPop 2025 + OpenStreetMap access analysis (six definitions; 300, 615 and 800 m).
Why it is low-hanging: Done: Claim Check 011 report and flyer (v1.2: split; the PN Gozo pledge is now CC-107).
Caveats: Draft pending right of reply (Partit Laburista / Government). Access analysis is a straight-line screening estimate. Manifesto translation is ours. The news summary narrowed the pledge to green space; the party's own text is assessed. Split on 5 Oct 2026; the PN's net-zero Gozo pledge is CC-107.
Notes: Report v1.3; pledge Not measurable; right of reply to send (draft; not for circulation before the deadline).

Claim and who made it: Public Works Ministry (Sept 2025): the sand and gravel laid on the Ta' Qali picnic area retains moisture, so 'the natural grass grows at a much faster rate well before the rainfall of the winter season'; park unit head Jason Micallef: grass would grow back with the winter rains. PM (Jan 2026): intervention after the spring concerts. PN and Momentum (Feb 2026): the gravel chokes the grass and could leave the area permanently barren.
Counter-evidence or context: Sentinel-2 (v1.1, reflectance offset applied): the 2.8 ha gravel zone (Momentum measured ~2.2 ha) greened every winter before the gravel (winter median NDVI 0.53-0.67 in 2023-2025, close to the rest of the park at 0.65-0.68) and stayed bare in winter 2025-26 (0.15) while the rest of the park was at 0.68. Summers were already bare before the gravel (~0.15), as the park management said. Gravel still in place and area bare in the last clear image, 27 Sep 2026. Soil-compaction reviews support the choking mechanism; gravel-sand mulch is a known water-conservation technique.
Test it against: Sentinel-2 NDVI and brightness 2023-2026 against a control area in the same park; soil compaction literature.
Why it is low-hanging: Done: Claim Check 012 report and flyer.
Body / actor: Public Works Ministry; Jason Micallef (Ta' Qali park unit); Prime Minister Robert Abela; Partit Nazzjonalista; Momentum
Caveats: Draft pending right of reply (Ministry, park unit, OPM, PN, Momentum). Verdict applies to the government assurance that grass would regrow; PN/Momentum description of the current state is supported, 'permanently' not shown. Intent and procurement not assessed. Works after 27 Sep 2026 not covered.
Notes: Report v1.1; verdict Contradicted (high); right of reply to send (draft; not for circulation before the deadline).

Short title: Permits keep property prices in check
Claim and who made it: Planning Authority CEO Johann Buttigieg (MaltaToday interview, 2 Mar 2025): continuing to issue permits helps keep property prices in check; without them Malta would face the same housing crises as other European countries. The interviewer cited about 91,000 dwellings approved over a decade.
Counter-evidence or context: Supported in direction by peer-reviewed research on supply constraints (Glaeser et al. 2005; Hilber and Vermeulen 2016; Saiz 2010); Anenberg and Kung (2020) find extra supply alone does little for rent burdens. Malta population +31% 2015-2025 (EU +2%; highest of 27, about 16 times the EU rate); real house prices +34% (EU +25%; Malta 2025 provisional), which ranks 16th of 27, below the median Member State (+41%); the EU aggregate is weighted towards Germany, France and Italy (49%). Rents (HICP actual rentals) +53% vs EU +21% (8th of 27); house prices +6.9% a year to 2026-Q2 (provisional) vs EU +4.7%. Housing-cost overburden rose from 1.1% (2015) to 2.9% (2022) while the EU's fell; Eurostat flags a break in Malta's series in 2023, after which it held at about 6% (6.0% in 2025; EU 7.7%). Overcrowding 4.7% vs EU 16.8%. 27.5% of dwellings not a main residence (Census 2021).
Test it against: Eurostat prc_hpi_a, tipsho10, demo_gind, ilc_lvho07a, ilc_lvho05a; all EU-27 demo_gind, tipsho10, prc_hicp_aind, prc_hpi_q, prc_hpi_cow; PA approved dwellings 2007-2025; NSO Census 2021; housing-supply literature.
Why it is low-hanging: Done: Claim Check 013 report and flyer.
Caveats: No right of reply needed (verdict Largely supported; a reply is sought only for Not substantiated, Misleading or Contradicted). Effect size unproven for Malta; affordability worsening; approvals are not completions. Prices only, not environmental costs of the permits.
Notes: Report v1.2; verdict Largely supported (moderate); no right of reply needed.

Claim and who made it: Planning Authority CEO Johann Buttigieg (Malta Independent, 7 Sep 2025): the PA once issued over 1,000 enforcement notices a year and now about 200, which he attributed to fewer illegalities; over 5,000 cases await direct action and 1,500 illegalities were removed by direct action in 30 years.
Counter-evidence or context: Notices fell 82% (1,033 a year in 2001-2009 to 187 in 2020-2024; PA annual reports give 164-233 a year in 2018-2024) while complaints of illegal development fell 11% since 2009 (2,701 to 2,411) and 35% since 2004/05, and averaged about 2,860 a year in 2017-2024, more than in 2009 or 2011 (2,105). Complaints confirmed as illegal development were about 1,280 in 2018 and about 1,200-1,250 in 2024; the fall of about a third since 2020 is measured from a 2020-21 peak (~1,820-1,880). Notices per 100 complaints fell from 29-41 (2005-2011) to 5-10 (2017-2024), and only 7-13 in every 100 confirmed cases ended in a notice in 2018-2024: most ended in a sanctioning application (497-818 a year) or removal by the owner. The PA's own reports explain the low number of notices as its strategy "to issue notices only where contraveners are uncooperative" (2018 p. 20; 2019 p. 18).
Test it against: MEPA annual reports 2004-2011; PA annual reports 2017-2023 (Issuu page images) and 2024; one news report of PA data (pending notices, end 2021); regulatory enforcement literature (context).
Why it is low-hanging: Done: Claim Check 014 report and flyer.
Caveats: Draft pending right of reply (Planning Authority). Figures accurate; verdict rests on the omitted change in how cases are handled. Complaints are a proxy for illegal building and their definition shifts (construction-site complaints separate in 2018, third-party-damage complaints included in 2019, anonymous reports stopped in 2024); confirmed cases are approximate (stated share x complaints received; the PA's bases differ and outcomes do not always add up). 2008 and 2012-2016 are missing, and notices halved between 2011 and 2017. Daily fines (since 2012) now apply to most notices, which may deter. v1.2 (5 Oct 2026) replaced second-hand 2019-2023 figures with the PA reports and added 2017-2018; verdict unchanged.
Notes: Report v1.2; verdict Misleading (moderate); right of reply to send (draft; not for circulation before the deadline).

Claim and who made it: Johann Buttigieg (planning conference, Sept 2026, as reported): when his 2019 chats with Yorgen Fenech took place he only had three weeks left at the Planning Authority. Campaigners say the business exchange dates from March 2019 and his tenure ended in October 2019.
Counter-evidence or context: Dates of the published chats and of the end of his first PA tenure are matters of record.
Test it against: Dates of the published chat messages against the documented end of his PA contract (2019). A document check only.
Why it is low-hanging: Two dates.
Caveats: Governance rather than environment: maintainer to confirm it is in scope. Date check only; no claims about motive or wrongdoing. Locate a recording or transcript of his exact words first.
Notes: Worker A, attempt 1 (2026-10-04): source: exact words not obtained (Newsbook paraphrases 'three weeks' outside quote marks; Maltese Herald 403; Times/MaltaToday/Independent refused; Wayback reset)

Claim and who made it: Infrastructure Malta (Shore-to-Ship project page, 1 Dec 2023): the Grand Harbour shore-to-ship initiative promises to slash 90% of air pollution in the Grand Harbour. Repeated at the inauguration (10 Jul 2024, cost given as EUR 33 million): completion means a 90% reduction, with 17,000 families around the harbour benefiting from cleaner air.
Counter-evidence or context: Connection is voluntary until 1 Jan 2030 (Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 Art. 6); Transport Malta: connecting 'remains the prerogative of the shipping line'. Transport Malta FOI records (via Amphora Media): 67 of 373 cruise berths (18%) plugged in from Jul 2024 to Jul 2025, 9% of berth time; 306 berths not plugged in; MSC World Europa made 35 of the 67 (35 of its 51 calls; all other ships 32 of 322, 10%); no stay of 2-4 days plugged in. MSC World Europa is LNG-powered (dual-fuel LNG / low-sulphur marine gasoil, MSC Cruises 2022), so when it runs on LNG the SOx and PM saving from plugging it in is smaller than the per-liner figures. Cruise calls rose from 357 (2024) to 385 (2025; calendar years, while uptake runs Jul-Jul). Infrastructure Malta's own 2020-2023 pages scope the 90% to the pollution cruise liners and Ro-Ro ships produce, with per-liner cuts on shore power of NO2 -93%, PM -92.6%, SO2 -99.6%, CO2 -39.6% (study not cited); the 2023 project page dropped that scope. Research context: hotelling is >90% of cruise CO2 in port (Mocerino et al. 2026); manoeuvring emissions remain (Gagic et al. 2022). Cost stated as EUR 33m (launch), 37m (phase 1) and 49.9m (whole project). No harbour air-quality study before and after.
Test it against: Transport Malta connection records (FOI, via Amphora Media); Valletta Cruise Port traffic; FuelEU Maritime Art. 6; peer-reviewed cruise emission inventories; MSC Cruises' ship description (v1.2).
Why it is low-hanging: Done: Claim Check 016 report and flyer.
Body / actor: Infrastructure Malta; Prime Minister Robert Abela; Ministry for Transport
Caveats: Right of reply to Infrastructure Malta and Transport Malta not yet sent. Connection figures second-hand (FOI reply not public); no later data than Jul 2025; no air-quality measurement either way. The per-liner cuts are Infrastructure Malta's own estimates. Which fuel MSC World Europa burned at berth in Valletta is not known. v1.2 (5 Oct 2026) added a figure of the 373 berths and the 90% per connected ship vs the 9% harbour-wide, and the ship's fuel; verdict and confidence unchanged. Maintainer decision (5 Oct 2026): sub-claim A rated Largely supported (was Plausible).
Notes: Report v1.2; verdict Misleading (moderate); right of reply to send (draft; not for circulation before the deadline).

Claim and who made it: Budget 2026 (27 Oct 2025): a reclamation project is already under way in the Freeport; the government is preparing to launch a large-scale land reclamation project outside the Freeport perimeter next year, for industrial and maritime use and to relocate certain commercial activities so other spaces can be enjoyed by families. In 2019 the Environment Minister said an EUR 11 million seabed study had found five or six sites that are 'possible and environmentally safe'.
Counter-evidence or context: Existing works confirmed: Sentinel-2 shows +3.7 ha (+/-1) at Terminal 2, 2023-2026 (stated ~30,000 m2, ~1 Mt inert fill). No site, size, cost, fill source, screening or call for the large-scale project found by 3 Oct 2026. Seabed study unpublished since 2019; budget lines EUR 500,000 (2023) -> 10,000 (2025). Short title: 830,000 m2 of land lost in five years
Claim and who made it: Amphora Media (Green to Grey, 11-12 Sep 2026): nearly 830,000 square metres of nature and cropland were built up in Malta between 2018 and 2023 (headline: 'over 830,000'), 0.26% of land; in nearly 95% of the take-up, farmland rather than natural area was affected.
Counter-evidence or context: v1.2: Amphora's published polygons (397) cover 828,429 m2, so 'nearly 830,000' is reproduced (the headline's 'over' is not). Spatial cross-check with Impact Observatory/Esri 10 m land cover (2017-2025): the model already maps 68% of Amphora's area as built-up in 2018 (61% in all of 2017-19), classes only 6-14% of it as newly built, and only 2-3% of its own new built-up land lies inside Amphora's polygons (5-7% within 20 m); its national net total ranges from -0.06 to 2.96 km2 depending on the rule and years. So the model measures different land and neither confirms nor rules out 0.83 km2 (v1.1 had read it as corroboration). 'Nearly 95%': cropland + grass = 96% (95.3-95.7%) of the area with a known 2018 class in Amphora's own data (our reading of the basis), counting Dynamic World 'grass' (which includes natural meadows) as farmland and leaving out the 37% of the area with no class; cropland alone is 22% of the whole. Two polygons (4,429 m2) were sea in 2018. Arithmetic (0.26%, 116 pitches, 1.94 km2 since 2006) checks out. EEA CORINE change maps: 20.6 ha (2006-12) and 93.7 ha (2012-18) of new artificial land, matching the 190,000 and 920,000 m2 quoted; changes under 5 ha are not mapped. Imagery spot-check (maintainer decision, 5 Oct 2026): 40 draws by systematic sampling proportional to area (seed 20261005, 39 polygons), checked by eye against Esri World Imagery Wayback (before Jul 2015-Aug 2016, 4 Sep 2018, 6 May 2023, Jun-Sep 2025): 72.5% of the sampled area confirmed open/green to grey (Wilson 95% CI 57-84%), 7.5% partial, 2.5% already grey, 0% still open, 17.5% unclear (15% being developed by Sep 2018); 55% (40-69%) confirmed and mostly grey by May 2023, so part of the figure is 2024-25 change. The imagery contradicts the model's 2018 built-up reading on these parcels. Land before: fields 59% (43-73%), 64% with orchards, the rest scrub, garrigue or rough grass, so 'nearly 95% farmland' is overstated. Verdict (maintainer decision, 5 Oct 2026): Not substantiated: about 456,000 m2 (330,000-574,000) was grey by May 2023 against 'nearly 830,000' for 2018-2023 (about 600,000 m2 by 2025), and about a third of the land was scrub or garrigue, not farmland.
Test it against: Amphora's published change polygons; imagery spot-check of 40 PPS draws against Esri World Imagery Wayback (2015-16, 2018, 2023, 2025); Impact Observatory LULC v2 (Planetary Computer 2017-2023, Esri 2017-2025); EEA CORINE change layers 2006-2012 and 2012-2018; OSM island areas; Amphora articles read in full.

The basis of the 95% is our reading, not confirmed by Amphora; the map file gives its years as 2018-2025, the article 2018-2023; class definitions differ between land-cover models.

Short title: EP study: noise law not the cause
Claim and who made it: Study for the European Parliament's Committee on Petitions (Ecocentric Consulting, February 2026): Malta's noise problems are not caused by how it transposed and implements the Environmental Noise Directive, with only two meaningful non-conformity issues, because the noise people complain about (construction, entertainment, neighbourhood) falls outside the Directive's scope; it cites a 2019 survey in which 21% of Maltese ranked noise among their top four environmental issues against an EU28 average of 9%.
Counter-evidence or context: The conclusion follows from the study's evidence. The Directive sets only reporting thresholds (55 dB Lden and 50 dB Lnight, above the WHO 2018 levels of 53 and 45 dB for roads and 45 and 40 dB for aircraft) and excludes construction, entertainment and neighbourhood noise. Eurostat (ilc_mddw01), an all-source self-reported measure that includes road traffic (which the Directive covers) and so shows the size of the problem, not its cause, puts Malta first in the EU for reported street or neighbour noise, 31.3% against 18.1% in 2023, above the EU average in all 12 available years since 2010. Action-plan delays (plan due January 2025 unpublished at January 2026) are a genuine END implementation issue. Legal compliance is not the same as exposure below WHO levels. The transposition table and infringement record were not independently verified. The WHO levels and the EEA exposure figures are second-hand via the study (the study, citing EEA, says the END figures are likely a considerable underestimation). The 21% vs 9% figure is in ERA's consultation annex (pp. 5-6, in the Office of the Superintendent of Public Health's comment, no survey named; annex read via Wayback on 6 Oct 2026); it is not in the Marmarà October 2019 survey summary (mean worry score for noise 3.90 of 5 only), so its origin is unidentified.
Test it against: Study text and transposition table; Eurostat ilc_mddw01 for Malta, EU-27 and all Member States; END thresholds against WHO 2018 levels as reported in the study; Crossref-verified WHO review literature.
Why it is low-hanging: Done: Claim Check 020 report and flyer.
Body / actor: Peter Hjerp and Clare Coffey (Ecocentric Consulting), study for the European Parliament Committee on Petitions (PE 783.089)
Caveats: The claimant is an EU body's commissioned study, not a Maltese speaker; the opinions are the authors', not the European Parliament's official position. The verdict covers legal conformity only, not whether Malta is quiet. Transposition table and infringement register not independently verified; the 21% vs 9% survey figure is in ERA's consultation annex (read via Wayback) but no survey is named and it is not in the Marmarà 2019 summary, so its origin is unidentified; sub-claim C rests on the study's own reading of the consultation and petition, not re-coded by us; WHO and EEA figures are second-hand via the study. No right of reply needed (verdict Largely supported; a reply is sought only for Not substantiated, Misleading or Contradicted).
Notes: Report v1.1; verdict Largely supported (moderate); no right of reply needed.

Claim and who made it: Government of Malta (COP30 national statement): Malta has reduced per-capita emissions by over 44% since 2005 and emissions per unit of GDP by more than 80%.
Counter-evidence or context: More than 80% per unit of GDP holds only at current prices (-82% to 2023, -84% to 2024). In chain-linked volumes the fall is -70% (2023) and -72% (2024); no year reaches -80%. The gap is a price effect (Malta GDP deflator +72% since 2005). The per-person fall (-46% / -48.5%) is the figure CC-003 checked; about half is population growth, total emissions fell 27% (EU 33%) and have risen 18% since the 2016 low. In the statement's favour: real GDP +161% with total emissions -27% is absolute decoupling, and Malta's fall exceeds the EU's on both intensity bases. On the residence basis (env_ac_ainah_r2: Malta-resident units, including international aviation fuel bought abroad) per-person emissions rose 69% from 2013 to 2024, rank 27 of 27 (EU-27 -21%); the claim's figures hold on the territorial (UNFCCC) basis (the statement names none), so this is context (CC-114).
Test it against: Eurostat env_air_gge, nama_10_gdp (current prices and chain-linked volumes) and nama_10_pe for Malta and the EU-27, recomputed with tools/cc-025-report/calc.py; CC-003 for the per-person figure.
Why it is low-hanging: Done: Claim Check 025 report and flyer.
Caveats: The wording is the paragraph supplied by the maintainer; our own download of the UNFCCC file was refused by a bot check, so it is not independently verified, and the rest of the statement may add context. The statement gives no year, scope or GDP basis; the choice of 2023 and 2024 is the report's assumption. A roughly ten-point overstatement on the usual (volumes) basis is a minor caveat because the 44% figure is right, the decoupling holds and current prices are a computable basis. On the residence basis (Eurostat air emissions accounts, env_ac_ainah_r2: Malta-resident units, including international aviation fuel bought abroad) per-person emissions rose 69% from 2013 to 2024, the largest rise of the 27 Member States (EU-27 -21%); the Government's figures hold on the territorial (UNFCCC) basis, though the statement names none, so this is context, not a contradiction (see CC-114, which differs because it draws a causal inference the data contradict). Largely supported: no right of reply needed. The speaker is attributed to the Government of Malta; the person who read the statement is not named in the document.

Claim and who made it: Environment and Resources Authority (Air Quality Plan for Malta 2025): the plan outlines actions that "have already yielded positive results for Malta's air quality"; the plan names them as measures that "have already contributed to improvements in air quality in Malta", such as power-sector reform, grants for more sustainable transport, free school transport, better ferry landing places, the fast ferry and free public transport for all.
Counter-evidence or context: Power-sector reform is shown to have helped: power-station sulphur oxides fell 99.8% in the reform years (2014-2018; 99.9% since 2008, but 55% of that fall came before 2015) and SO2 in the air fell 83% at Żejtun (2008-12 to 2018-23, leaving out 2011 with 28.5% of the year measured; the ships' fuel-sulphur cap of 1 January 2020 is a co-driver the data cannot separate); SO2 at Kordin was already 2.6 µg/m³ in 2014, before the reform. NO2 and PM2.5 at the Msida roadside fell 22% and 17% (2015-17 to 2021-23; NO2 -20% to 2022-23 alone), in step with a cleaner fleet, but no named transport measure is shown to have caused it. PM10 at Msida, the reason for the plan, did not improve: after ERA's natural-source deduction 2023 had 52 days over the limit (35 allowed), the most of 2015-2023 at the old Msida point (ERA's 2024-25 zone counts, 20 and 23, come from other stations and are not comparable), after free school transport, the fast ferry and free public transport began; a single-site, single-year comparison with no weather adjustment. The plan gives uptake or passenger figures, not air-quality effects, for grants, ferry landing places, the fast ferry and free public transport (plan pages 3, 21-67, 91 and 95 read; pp. 4-20, 68-90 and 96-104 skimmed for effect estimates, none found). Its one test (free school transport, NO2 "around 10 µg/m³" lower at rush hour) does not reproduce in validated data: the peak falls by 1.0 µg/m³ (62.3 to 61.3 at Start 07; +0.7 on weekdays only); the plan's 2018-19 curves reproduce only with hour-ending labels and its 2014-17 baseline does not reproduce under either labelling, so its gap sits in the baseline. A sustained fall of 11.5 µg/m³ in October-December weekday-morning NO2 (2013-17 to 2019-23) began in 2019, not 2018, and cannot be tied to the measure. In the 12 months after free public transport began, 10 of 11 station readings were higher than in the 12 months before.
Test it against: EEA validated station data (AirBase, E1a) for PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2 and CO at every ERA station, 2006-2025; ERA's attainment reports (dataflow G) 2015-2025; Eurostat env_air_emis and road_eqs_carpda; traffic site vs background stations; before/after windows around each dated measure; the plan's own school-transport comparison recomputed, with a test of the hour labels of its Figure 26 against the EEA hourly profiles (tools/cc-034-report/ calc.py, digitise_fig26.py, data/cc-034/checks.csv).

Missing evidence, not evidence against: flat PM10 does not prove the measures did nothing (car numbers +31%, 2013-2025). No weather normalisation or traffic data; the 2023 PM10 count and the +8.1 µg/m³ after free public transport are single-site, single-year comparisons; the Msida monitor moved about 300 m in January 2024, so 2024-25 are not compared with earlier years, and the Msida Creek works lie 112 m from the old point (when work near it began is not verified). Claim and who made it: European Environment Agency (Air pollution quick country facts, 2025 country fact sheets): in Malta the rate of all-cause natural deaths attributable to long-term exposure to PM2.5 above 5 µg/m³, per 100 000 inhabitants aged 30 or over, is estimated to have fallen by 67.7% between 2005 and 2023 (from 143.5 to 46.3), resulting in 172 (95% CI 131-192) attributable deaths in 2023.
Counter-evidence or context: Every figure reproduces from the EEA's own burden-of-disease table and Eurostat sdg_11_52, which republishes it (143.5, 46.3, 67.74%, 172 (131-192)); the ETC HE technical report gives 173 (132-193), a one-death difference we cannot explain. From Eurostat natural deaths aged 30+ and the EEA's concentrations we get 346 (2005) and 170 (2023) deaths, within 1.2%. Measured PM2.5 fell: Msida -39% (2007-2023) and the three long-running stations -25% (2010-2023); this is direct evidence of a fall, not a check of the map, which is built on these stations. Caveats: no Maltese PM2.5 was reported to the EEA for 2005 (first valid day 29 August 2006), so the 2005 value (21.0 µg/m³) is a map value, from an older map method and model than 2023; the 95% CI covers the risk function only. PM10 at Msida and Żejtun did not fall while PM2.5 fell about 40%, and the PM2.5 instruments changed. The number of deaths fell 50.6% (348 to 172), as the population aged 30+ grew 54%; counting all concentrations the rate fell 54.7%, and from 2007 it fell 56.6%.
Test it against: EEA burden-of-disease table (Malta, all scenarios; EU-27; all countries), Eurostat sdg_11_52, demo_pjan, demo_magec, hlth_cd_aro and env_air_emis, recomputed with tools/cc-035-report/calc.py; the EEA's briefing, indicator and ETC technical and map reports for the method; EEA AirBase and E1a station files for Malta's measured PM2.5 and PM10.
Why it is low-hanging: Done: Claim Check 035 report and flyer.
Caveats: The statement is the EEA's modelled estimate, reported accurately. Its 2005 starting value is a map value: no Maltese PM2.5 was reported to the EEA for 2005 (the first valid day is in August 2006), the 2005 and 2023 maps come from different methods and models, and the 95% CI leaves exposure error out, so the exact 67.7% is less certain than its decimal suggests. Measured PM2.5 fell from 2007, but the maps are built on the stations, so the stations do not check the map. It is a rate per person aged 30+; the number of deaths fell by about half. Largely supported verdict: no right of reply needed.
Notes: Report v1.0; verdict Largely supported (high); no right of reply needed.

Short title: PN: afforestation in a net-zero Gozo
Claim and who made it: PN programme 2026 (Nifs Ġdid, in Maltese; our translation), chapter Għawdex, item 46: a plan so that by 2040 Gozo becomes a Net-Zero Island, "where every unit of emissions generated is reduced or offset" by initiatives such as solar panels, electric vehicles, building efficiency, ecological restoration, "afforestation" and water and soil conservation, "among others". The environment chapter adds "more afforestation and open spaces in both Malta and Gozo" (item 01) and tree planting and afforestation against heat, flooding and pollution (item 20). News summaries said Gozo would become net zero "through afforestation" and reported a national indigenous-tree strategy; neither is in the programme.
Counter-evidence or context: The programme lists afforestation among the ways Gozo's emissions would be "reduced or offset" by 2040 but gives no area, number of trees, species, sites, carbon rate or date. Offsetting Gozo's energy CO2 (118,333-153,997 t a year in 2016-2020, a study for the EU islands secretariat) by trees alone would need new forest 4.9-6.3 times Gozo's 67 km2 at a rate measured in the Yatir pine forest (3.62 t CO2/ha a year), 2.3-3.0 times at a review's plantation rate (7.6 t) and 19-25 times at the rate measured for native oaks in Spain (0.92 t). CORINE 2018 maps no forest on Gozo; planting all of its semi-natural land (1,265 ha, mostly garrigue and maquis, 36% of it in Natura 2000 sites) would offset 3.0-3.9% (0.8-8.1% across rates). Malta's whole forest is 470 ha (FAO definition, 2025); Malta's water exploitation index was 30% in 2023 (Eurostat: permanent water scarcity); 20-year survival of planted pines was 30-58% in an arid Spanish trial. No indigenous-tree strategy appears in the programme's 16 chapters; "indigenous" is used once, for farm varieties and breeds. "Through afforestation" is a news summary, not the PN's wording.

Short title: Commission: Malta to emit more in 2030 than in 2005
Claim and who made it: European Commission (EU Climate Action Progress Report 2025, COM(2025) 668, 6 Nov 2025): before any use of flexibilities, Malta's projected 2030 effort-sharing emissions leave a gap of 49 and 61 percentage points to its 19% reduction target, so Malta "is projected to emit more in 2030 than in 2005"; Malta is among the Member States with the largest projected gaps and (after banking, borrowing and the ETS flexibility) is projected to have excess emissions in 2026-2030. The Commission adds that, given the EU-wide surplus, it "cannot, at this stage, conclude" that Member States, taken together, are not making sufficient progress.
Counter-evidence or context: Reproduced. Malta's March 2025 projections (EEA) give 1,323.8 kt with planned measures and 1,450.1 kt with existing ones in 2030, against the legal 2005 level of 1,020.6 kt: +29.7% and +42.1%, gaps of 48.7 and 61.1 points to -19%. Above 2005 against every 2005 figure (EEA estimate 1,007.4 kt; 2013-2020 base year 1,116.1 kt: +18.6% at least) and with projections re-based on reviewed 2023 emissions (+26% / +38%). 2024 approximated emissions +40.8% (1,437 kt); over the yearly limit by 220, 257 and 301 kt in 2022-2024. Gap ranking with planned measures: Malta 48.7, Ireland 20.3, Germany 13.2 points (in tonnes Malta 0.5 Mt, Germany 64 Mt). Context and the other side: 2021-2030 balance -2.09 Mt (planned measures); the ETS flexibility (0.51 Mt) and the maximum land-use credit (0.03 Mt) leave 1.55 Mt to buy from other Member States (about 1% of the 125-175 Mt EU surplus) or cut; no safety reserve for Malta (Decision 2023/863). The Commission says it "cannot, at this stage, conclude" that Member States are not making sufficient progress. Malta's plan says the target rests on 2005 forecasts overtaken by population growth (the -19% was in fact set in 2018 on the basis of GDP per capita, with 2005 as the base year; population +41% to 2024; effort-sharing emissions per person flat at 2.53 t), and EU law (Regulation 2023/857) accepts the target is above Malta's cost-effective potential. "Missing its target" was the intake's paraphrase, not the Commission's wording.
Test it against: EEA effort-sharing emissions 2005-2024 and GHG projections (2025 and 2023 submissions) for Malta and all EU-27; 2005 levels, targets, allocations and flexibilities from Regulations (EU) 2018/842 and 2023/857 and Implementing Decisions (EU) 2020/2126, 2024/1884 and 2026/895; Commission SWD Tables 25-26; recomputed in tools/cc-094-report/calc.py.

Short title: EU: no registration or prior authorisation of water abstraction in Malta
Claim and who made it: European Commission (July infringements package, 8 July 2026, summarising its letter of formal notice INFR(2026)2115): Malta has failed to put in place a registration requirement for surface water abstraction and a prior authorisation regime to control the abstraction of surface and groundwater; in addition, Maltese law does not ensure a periodic review of the controls over the abstraction of surface and groundwater having a significant impact on water bodies.
Counter-evidence or context: Malta controls groundwater sources in several ways: every source had to be notified by 20 Nov 2008 (S.L. 549.164; a later route exists for some old sources), drilling is under a moratorium with exceptions (S.L. 549.165), metering is required (S.L. 549.166), and ERA can order a source closed or its abstraction cut. Malta reports (April 2025) that "Only these registered sources are permitted to extract groundwater" and that most registered sources are metered; in 2019 it told the Commission that more than 3 000 private sources were metered; and in 2019 Commission staff described "a concession, authorisation and/or permitting regime to control groundwater and a register of groundwater use" (SWD(2019) 48). S.L. 549.100 reg. 12(3)(e) repeats the Directive's duty to review abstraction controls. Against that: S.L. 549.164 reg. 6 and S.L. 549.165 reg. 9 say notification and drilling permits give no right to draw water, we found no instrument that authorises abstraction, and the Government's 2023 Green Paper and Measure 053 of the 3rd plan treat an abstraction permit as still to be created (none found in force on 6 Oct 2026).
Test it against: Water Framework Directive Art. 11(3)(e), 11(5), 11(7) and 24; Maltese law on legislation.mt (S.L. 549.100, 549.164-549.166, 549.168, 549.172, 549.21, 549.53, 549.155, 545.14, 545.02, Cap. 549, Cap. 355), the titles of all 2024-2026 Legal Notices, the text of all 2024-2026 Acts and the titles of S.L. 549, 423, 545, 355 and 427; the 2023 Green Paper, Malta's April 2025 interim report and 2nd water plan; Commission SWD(2019) 48, COM(2025) 2 and SWD(2025) 13; Eurostat env_wat_abs and EEA WISE 2022 reporting, recomputed with tools/cc-101-report/calc.py.
Why it is low-hanging: Done: Claim Check 101 report and flyer.
Data readiness: High: Commission text, legislation.mt, EWA documents, Eurostat and WISE readable; ERA and the 3rd RBMP refuse scripts.
Caveats: Largely supported: no right of reply needed. The verdict covers the Commission's first sentence (registration of surface-water abstraction; prior authorisation to control abstraction), rated on the facts we could check (no register of surface-water abstraction and no permit to abstract water in the instruments read). The second sentence (periodic review, sub-claim D) and whether a register of groundwater sources amounts to a "prior authorisation regime" are legal questions and are not rated; sub-claim A (what the Directive requires) is the Commission's premise and is not rated. No legal opinion is given. The claim is the Commission's published summary; the letter of formal notice and Malta's reply are not public. "Not found" statements rest on a bounded search listed in literature/CC-101/notes.md (instruments read, titles of 943 Legal Notices, text of 101 Acts and titles of 344 subsidiary instruments; none found in force on 6 Oct 2026). The record's title condenses the Commission's first sentence and is not itself rated; Malta issues permits to drill boreholes, not to abstract water. Do not read the notice as evidence of actual over-abstraction; groundwater status is in CC-009 and CC-047.
Notes: Report v1.0; verdict Largely supported (moderate); no right of reply needed.

Short title: ADPD: no study of Freeport and airport noise

The 45% reproduces exactly as the rise in transport emissions (+45.0% on approximated 2024 data, 0.528 to 0.766 Mt; +48.4% on the final inventory); the share barely moved (52.0% to 53.3%). Footnote (140) and Table A8.1 call the sector "road transport", but the table's series includes domestic shipping (11.9% of it in 2024, +184% since 2005). 2024 values are approximated; final data after the 2027 review.
Test it against: Eurostat env_air_gge (2026 inventory, Malta and EU-27, CRF 1.A.3 and sub-categories); EEA ESR emissions 2005-2024 and approximated inventory 2024; EEA GovReg 2026 v1.0; the report's Graph 3.1 read from the PDF's vector paths; Commission CAPR 2024 and 2025 Malta profiles; 2025 Country Report; Regulation (EU) 2018/842 Art. 2 as amended by 2023/857; Implementing Decision (EU) 2020/2126 Annex I (2005 base). Recomputed in tools/cc-109-report/calc.py.

Data readiness: High: EEA datasets, Eurostat and both copies of the report read on 6 Oct 2026.

Short title: EEA: Malta among highest fossil-fuel subsidies relative to GDP
Claim and who made it: European Environment Agency (indicator page, 29 Jan 2025): in 2023 fossil-fuel subsidies represented the highest shares of GDP in Malta, Poland and Slovakia, all at or above 1.5%.

Malta's 2023 figure (EUR 605m, or 633m with a stand-in) is 96% one line, compensation to Enemalta for frozen energy prices, booked as actual costs and wholly to natural gas; it is 2.1 times the IMF Article IV energy-subsidy cost for 2023 (1.4% of GDP, CR 26/29) and 1.7 times the Government's expected cost (1.7% of GDP, DBP 2024, other basic commodities included), a gap we could not reconcile. The IMF's price-gap database records no explicit subsidy for Malta; the OECD/IISD tracker has no OECD or IEA estimate for Malta. Malta was 0.08-0.10% of GDP in 2015-2020 (24th-27th of 27) and is first again for 2024 in COM(2026) 472. In euros Malta's EUR 0.63bn is 19th of 27.
Test it against: Commission subsidy inventory 2024 edition (CIRCABC) rebuilt measure by measure (locally); EEA chart data; COM(2025) 17 Figure 16 (read by pixel); Eurostat nama_10_gdp, gov_10a_main and nrg_cb_e; Malta Draft Budgetary Plans 2024 and 2025; IMF CR 26/29 Table 2 (read for CC-018/CC-022); IMF Fossil Fuel Subsidies Data 2023 update; OECD/IISD Fossil Fuel Subsidy Tracker; COM(2026) 472; ECFIN Discussion Paper 214 for definitions (tools/cc-113-report/calc.py).

Versions C and D (unconfirmed items set to zero) are a lower bound, not equally valid versions; B and D use Eurostat GDP as of 6 Oct 2026, which the EEA could not have had. COM(2025) 17 (28 Jan 2025) was read from the EU Publications Office: its Figure 16 gives the same top four as the CIRCABC file, which was modified on 9 Apr 2025. The Commission workbook is (c) Enerdata (reproduction prohibited without written permission): measure rows are not committed. The original 29 Jan 2025 page could not be opened; the earliest copy read is 3 Feb 2025. IMF CR 26/29 figures are from the CC-018/CC-022 record (read in full 5 Oct 2026). Short title: PN: only EU state with rising emissions intensity
Claim and who made it: Nationalist Party press release signed by Shadow Minister Eve Borg Bonello (26 Jan 2026; in Maltese, our translation), citing Eurostat: "Malta is the only EU Member State which, instead of reducing, increased the intensity of greenhouse gas emissions from 2013 to date. Malta in fact increased these emissions by 17%, when the average intensity of these emissions in all EU Member States fell by 34%"; "In simple words, it is not simply that we are polluting more because the economy grew, but today, for every euro we put into our economy, we are polluting more than we were polluting in 2013"; and "This is the direct result of a lack of ambition on the part of the Maltese Government on several fronts. Among them, the clear lack of ambition to seriously increase the use of renewable energy." The release also says Estonia "reduced emissions by 64%", Ireland "by 50%" and Finland "by 44%", and that Malta generated "only 10.7%" of its energy from renewables in 2024 when the European average is "a little over 25%", "third from last".
Counter-evidence or context: Eurostat's figure is quoted correctly (January release +16.6%, EU -34.0%; August 2026 data +14.3%, still the only rise; Malta 27th of 27 from every base year 2008-2023; EU-27 values flagged i), but it is a residence-based measure. Malta's resident production units emitted 2.78 Mt CO2e in 2013 and 6.59 Mt in 2024; air transport rose from 0.30 to 4.73 Mt (71.8% of 2024; 2024 estimate, Eurostat flag i), 116% of the net rise in resident-unit emissions (+3.81 Mt; a share of that rise, not of the intensity indicator); in intensity terms air transport alone went from about 36 g/EUR in 2013 to about 266 g/EUR in 2024 (estimate). All of the rise is fuel bought abroad by resident air transport firms (Eurostat bridging table: 299 of 304 kt in 2013, 100% of the 2024 estimate). The NSO attributes the 2023 jump to airlines that started operating that year. Without air-transport emissions the indicator fell from every base year 2008-2023 (-8.5% to -72%): -64.0% since 2013 (2nd-largest fall in the EU; EU -35.2%) but -29.5% since 2016 (17th of 27; EU -30.1%). The territorial inventory per euro of GDP also fell from every base year (-6.6% to -69%): -61.3% since 2013 (2nd after Estonia; EU -35.5%), -27.1% since 2016 (21st; EU -29.8%). Most of the fall came in 2014-2016, when electricity-sector emissions fell from 1,703 to 581 kt (743 kt in 2024, +28% since 2016), so these counter-figures depend on the base year too; in the PN's favour, from base years 2014-2019 Malta's rise is +19.5% to +97%. More renewable electricity, on its own, could not have removed the rise: electricity-sector emissions fell about 56% (1,703 to 743 kt), and with zero electricity-sector emissions in 2024 the indicator would still be 1.4% above 2013 (329.8 against 325.2 g/EUR); this bound tests electricity (NACE D) only. Renewable shares rose over the period (electricity 1.6% to 10.7%, overall 3.8% to 17.2%). The release's next paragraph also cites traffic; households' own car use is outside the indicator. With 2013 as base Malta is the only riser only for end year 2024, a Eurostat estimate; 2013-2023 it fell 8.3% and no state rose. Estonia, Ireland and Finland cut intensity, not emissions: residence accounts / territorial inventory 2013-2024, Estonia -55.4% / -53.1% (2024 flagged i), Finland -37.9% / -37.6% (i), Ireland +13.7% / -6.9% (flagged e; its air transport, 9.90 to 16.32 Mt, is 87% of its residence-based rise). On the residence basis the PN used, emissions per person rose 69.2% 2013-2024 (27th of 27; EU -21.2%). 10.7% is Malta's renewable share of electricity (EU 47.5%); its overall share is 17.2%, fourth from last (EU 25.2%); Eurostat's release of 18 Dec 2025 named Belgium, Luxembourg and Ireland as the lowest three. In the PN's favour: the statistic is real and Eurostat's own news item gives no explanation either; Malta's renewable shares are among the EU's lowest.
